meta.title: Who really said "The moment you know how your suffering came to be, you are already on the path of release from it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the Buddha. The sentence is Thích Nhất Hạnh’s, condensed from his 1996 Dharma talk — and the canonical passage behind it is spoken by Sāriputta.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The moment you know how your suffering came to be, you are already on the path of release from it'?
meta.ogDescription: Thích Nhất Hạnh paraphrased the Buddha in a 1996 talk. A later book printed the condensed version inside quotation marks, and it has travelled as scripture ever since.

answer.label: Not the Buddha — Thích Nhất Hạnh’s wording
answer.authorDates: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Zen monk, teacher and peace activist
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears inside quotation marks, attributed to the Buddha, in Thích Nhất Hạnh’s The Heart of the Buddha’s Teaching. It began as his own paraphrase. In a Dharma talk given at Plum Village on 4 August 1996 ↗ he said: “If you already see the nature of your suffering, how it has come to be, you are already on your way to liberation” — and then added, in his own voice, “That is a sentence uttered by the Buddha.” The discourse behind it, on Bodhipaksa’s reading, is Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.31 ↗, where the words about seeing “this has come to be” are spoken not by the Buddha but by his disciple Sāriputta.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Heart of the Buddha’s Teaching
New York: Broadway Books, 1999, per Wikipedia’s bibliography; Bodhipaksa cites p. 45 without naming his edition
“The Five-Fold Steps of Training,” Plum Village, France, 4 August 1996
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.31 — the words are Sāriputta’s

source.excerpt: How that suffering has come to be, that is the second truth. That is about the nature of your suffering. If you already see the nature of your suffering, how it has come to be, you are already on your way to liberation. That is a sentence uttered by the Buddha.
trail: Thích Nhất Hạnh’s talk “The Five-Fold Steps of Training” is published by Plum Village with the header “Dharma Talk given by Thich Nhat Hanh on August 4th, 1996 in Plum Village, France,” and opens “Today is the fourth of August, 1996.” The paraphrase, and his own framing of it as something the Buddha said, are both in that transcript ↗.

The discourse behind the paraphrase is Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.31, “What Has Come to Be” ↗. The Blessed One puts the question; the answer — “one sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This has come to be’… one is practising for the purpose of revulsion towards what has come to be, for its fading away and cessation” — is Venerable Sāriputta’s.

The Buddhist teacher Bodhipaksa set out the whole chain on Fake Buddha Quotes, quoting the book’s wording, the 1996 talk and the sutta side by side and concluding that this “isn’t a quote from the Buddha” — his page on the line (archived 22 May 2024) ↗. He is the source for the page number, 45.
The book itself is catalogued at the Internet Archive as The Heart of the Buddha’s Teaching ↗; Wikipedia’s bibliography for Thích Nhất Hạnh lists it as Broadway Books, 1999, ISBN 0-7679-0369-2 ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is Thích Nhất Hạnh speaking in his own voice and reporting what he took the Buddha to have taught — “that is a sentence uttered by the Buddha” — not transcribing one. The book version compresses the whole passage into a single sentence and sets it inside quotation marks.

source.rightsNote: Nothing here is public domain. The wording is a twentieth-century composition: the talk was given in 1996 and is posted by Plum Village under a © Thich Nhat Hanh notice, and The Heart of the Buddha’s Teaching was published in 1999. The ancient discourse behind it is long out of copyright, but these are not its words.

author.name: Thích Nhất Hạnh
author.heading: Who Thích Nhất Hạnh was
author.metaLine: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Zen monk, teacher and peace activist
author.bio: Thích Nhất Hạnh was ordained in Vietnam at sixteen and spent the war years arguing for a Buddhism that acted in the world — work that got him exiled for nearly four decades and earned him a Nobel Peace Prize nomination from Martin Luther King Jr. From Plum Village, the community he founded in south-west France, he gave Dharma talks in English that were transcribed and edited into more than a hundred books. That pipeline is exactly how this sentence happened: he told an audience what the Buddha taught, and somewhere between the microphone and the page his summary acquired quotation marks.

Canonical parallel: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.31, where the passage is spoken by Sāriputta.

copyAttribution: "The moment you know how your suffering came to be, you are already on the path of release from it." — Not the Buddha. Thích Nhất Hạnh, The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching (New York: Broadway Books, 1999), where it is printed as a Buddha quotation; Bodhipaksa locates it at p. 45 without naming his edition. It condenses a longer paraphrase from his Dharma talk of 4 August 1996. The canonical passage behind it, Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.31, is spoken by the Buddha's disciple Sāriputta. Traced by Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: How a paraphrase acquired quotation marks
misattribution.intro: The line travels as scripture. It is a twentieth-century summary of scripture, made by a man who said so at the time.

items.why: No discourse in the Pali Canon contains this sentence. The passage it derives from, Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.31 ↗, does not say that knowing how suffering came to be puts you on the path of release; it says that seeing “this has come to be” with correct wisdom is practice for the fading away and cessation of what has come to be — and it is Sāriputta, not the Buddha, who says it.

items.who: Thích Nhất Hạnh, Plum Village, 4 August 1996
items.why: In the talk he says “If you already see the nature of your suffering, how it has come to be, you are already on your way to liberation,” then adds “That is a sentence uttered by the Buddha.” The transcript is on Plum Village’s own site ↗. The reporting frame is the part that later disappeared.

misattribution.truthLine: The Buddha did teach that suffering has knowable causes and that seeing them is the way out — that is the second and third of the Four Noble Truths. He did not put it in these words, and neither, strictly, did Thích Nhất Hạnh: Bodhipaksa’s reconstruction ↗ has an editor turning “the Buddha said that…” into “the Buddha said: ‘…’” somewhere between the talk and the book.

context.heading: Why this one is easy to believe
lead: The sentence is doing real Buddhist work. Look at the Four Noble Truths and the structure is right there: there is suffering, suffering has an origin, the origin can cease, and there is a path. Knowing how your suffering came to be really is, in that scheme, the hinge between the second truth and the third. So the line passes the sniff test that stops most fake Buddha quotes — it is not sentimental, it is not self-help, and it is not saying anything the tradition would disown.

What it fails is the transcription test. The Pali discourses are formulaic and repetitive by design, built to be memorised and recited; they do not produce clean aphorisms like this one. “The moment you know…” is the cadence of a modern teacher talking to a room, and that is exactly what it was.
detailsBody: Step one, the canon: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.31 ↗. The Buddha asks Sāriputta a question about the Parayana verses; Sāriputta, after three silences, answers with the “this has come to be” formula about seeing origination through nutriment.

Step two, the talk: on 4 August 1996 at Plum Village, Thích Nhất Hạnh renders that idea in his own English — suffering as something you feed, seeing the food as the way out — and attributes the thought to the Buddha in reported speech.

Step three, the book: The Heart of the Buddha’s Teaching prints the compressed version with a colon and quotation marks. Nothing dishonest happened at any step; a reporting clause just got lost in editing, and a paraphrase became a quotation.
context.pull: It is a fair summary of the Buddha. It is not a sentence of his.

sourcesVerified.claim: Bodhipaksa concludes the line is not a Buddha quote, traces it to Thích Nhất Hạnh and gives p. 45 of The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching.
The 4 August 1996 Plum Village talk contains the longer paraphrase and the words "That is a sentence uttered by the Buddha."
In SN 12.31 the "this has come to be" passage is spoken by Venerable Sāriputta, in answer to the Blessed One.
Wikipedia gives Thích Nhất Hạnh's dates as 11 October 1926 – 22 January 2022 and lists The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching as Broadway Books, 1999.
The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching (Harmony Books, 2015 reissue).
